author: Dr. Michael Lee - Health Editor
title: Dr. Mohamed Warsame Dualeh: Pioneer in Refugee Health and Humanitarian Leader Remembered
text:
Dr. Mohamed Warsame Dualeh, a pioneering Somali physician who reshaped refugee camp health management across the Horn of Africa, died on April 26, 2026, in Lüneberg, Germany, at the age of 72 following a cerebral stroke, according to reporting by World Hunger News.
Key Clinical Takeaways:
Dr. Dualeh served as Director of the Somalia Refugee Health Unit and Head of Operations in Darfur for the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR). He earned his Master of Public Health from the University of Sydney, focusing his thesis on community-based maternal and child care for diarrheal diseases. His early operational frameworks in Somali refugee camps helped establish epidemiological surveillance standards later mirrored globally, including principles adopted in the Sphere Handbook. Born on April 14, 1954, in Hargeisa, Somalia, Dr. Dualeh graduated with distinction from the Benadir Medical School in Mogadishu. According to colleague Dr. Ahmed Magan, as cited by World Hunger News, Dr. Dualeh belonged to a generation of Somali medical professionals whose clinical practice became inextricably linked to conflict, mass population displacement, and humanitarian response. His early foundational work centered on the Refugee Health Unit (RHU) in Mogadishu, which coordinated care protocols for approximately one million Ethiopian refugees who had fled to Somalia across roughly 35 camps.
Before Dr. Dualeh and his contemporaries introduced community-based primary healthcare models, humanitarian medical interventions relied heavily on top-down approaches directed by foreign professionals. Mike Toole, former senior medical adviser in the RHU within the Somali Ministry of Health, noted that Dr. Dualeh was a major force in basing national refugee health programs on epidemiological evidence, prevention, and active community participation. Beverly Snell highlighted that this decentralized model proved so effective among refugee populations that local host communities began utilizing the framework, creating a dual-access public health standard that heavily influenced international guidelines.
He directed operations in Darfur for the UNHCR, managed complex humanitarian deployments throughout the Horn of Africa, and officially retired from international civil service in 2014. Following his retirement, he served as an adviser to the President's office in Somaliland, working to organize regional public health infrastructure and advocate for international recognition. He continued offering his public health expertise to United Nations initiatives into 2025.
For institutions deploying medical teams to high-risk environments, structured operational frameworks are vital to reducing morbidity and mortality rates among displaced populations.
Photo: worldhunger.org Dr. Dualeh is survived by his wife, Marie Therese Lenz, and children, Amalie, Issa, and Edna. His academic contributions, particularly regarding childhood diarrheal disease management and serial nutritional surveillance in vulnerable populations, remain foundational references for modern humanitarian medicine.
